subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Maheshwar Dialogue

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 125–128): read the full Aarav–Ananya–Chachi dialogue aloud.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or draws attention to the newspaper-and-fort scene that opens the chapter. She asks students what they see and what they already know about forts, building curiosity before the text is opened.
Let us Read (pp. 125–128) — teacher reads the entire dialogue aloud with expressive voice differentiation for Aarav, Ananya, and Chachi. Students follow in their textbooks.
Let us Read (pp. 125–128) — students take turns reading the dialogue in threes, each student voicing one character. Teacher coaches pronunciation of Maheshwar, Ahilya Bai, Holkar, and Narmada.
Teacher leads a quick whole-class retell: she pauses at key moments and invites students to supply the next piece of information — what Chachi said about the fort's stones, the river, the queen.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at Grade IV often rush through dialogue reading without character distinction; insist on one voice per character so the conversational texture of the chapter comes through. The names Ahilya Bai, Holkar, and Narmada carry unfamiliar phoneme clusters — model each slowly before the student turn. Any student who struggles with the longer turns may share the role with a partner.
materials: Blackboard or chart with character names: Aarav, Ananya, Chachi

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Deep-Dive: Thinking About the Dialogue

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 128): discuss all four short-answer questions about Ahilya Bai, fort location, materials, and the statue.

time_bands.activity: Having read the dialogue aloud together, teacher invites two or three students to retell what Chachi told the children — the fort, the queen, the stones — in their own words. This surfaces prior reading without requiring a new read-through.

Let us Think A (p. 128) — teacher reads Question 1 (Who was Ahilya Bai?) and Question 2 (Where is Maheshwar Fort located and what makes its location special?) aloud. Students locate evidence in the dialogue text and respond in pairs before sharing with the class.

Let us Think A (p. 128) — teacher reads Question 3 (materials used to build the fort and their origins) and Question 4 (what the statue of Queen Ahilya Bai represents). Students write brief answers in their notebooks; teacher circulates and prompts with guiding questions.

Class shares answers for all four questions. Teacher builds a simple summary on the board: Queen Ahilya Bai | Fort location | Building materials | The statue. Students check and correct their own notebook entries.

periods.teacher_notes: The dialogue tells students that the red stones came from Gujarat and Rajasthan — students commonly confuse the source state with Madhya Pradesh; draw attention to that sentence explicitly. For Question 4, Chachi says the statue stands 13 feet tall in front of the palace — guide students to connect the statue's scale with respect and remembrance, not just physical size.

periods.activity_title: Discussion: Why Do Historical Places Excite Us?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 129): discuss both oral prompts — why historical places are interesting and which part of the fort students would most want to see.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the chapter's situation: Aarav and Ananya grew more and more excited as Chachi described the fort's balconies, the statue, and the temples. She asks the class to close their eyes and picture standing at the fort gate.

Let us Think B (p. 129) — Prompt 1: 'What do you think makes historical places like Maheshwar Fort interesting?' Students think for one minute, then share in pairs. Teacher selects four or five pairs to share with the whole class and records key ideas on the board.

Let us Think B (p. 129) — Prompt 2: 'If you were Aarav or Ananya, which part of the fort would you most want to see — the overhanging balconies, the statue, or the temples? Why?' Students choose their preference and justify it orally in small groups of three.

Each group's spokesperson shares the group's most interesting reason. Teacher invites brief whole-class agreement or counter-response. She closes by noting that Chachi promised to take the children — and by extension, this class — to discover the fort's secrets.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often give single-word reasons ('it's old', 'it's big') — push for connected reasoning by asking 'why does that make it interesting to you?' after each response. The two prompts build on each other: the first is general, the second is personal; keep them in that order so students move from shared thinking to individual voice.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Sequence: The Story of Maheshwari Sarees

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 131): teacher reads the Maheshwari sarees passage; students arrange four sentences in sequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task: the chapter mentions Maheshwari sarees as the town's other famous gift. She writes the four jumbled sentences on the board and asks students to read them silently before listening.

Let us Listen (p. 131) — teacher reads the transcript passage aloud slowly and clearly (first reading). Students listen with books closed, attending to the order of events: pure silk → cotton introduced → reversible borders → national and international markets.

Let us Listen (p. 131) — teacher reads the passage a second time, then a third. After each reading, students may update their sequencing attempt in their notebooks. Teacher pauses briefly after each sentence on the third reading.

Students write their final sequence (c, a, d, b) in notebooks and compare with a partner. Class discusses: teacher asks a student to read the first sentence that should appear and builds the correct order collaboratively on the board.
Teacher reads the passage a final time, students follow the correct sequence on the board. She asks one volunteer to say in one sentence what Maheshwari sarees are famous for.

periods.teacher_notes: The correct order is: the weavers originally used pure silk → later a blend of silk and cotton → famous for reversible borders → available in India and other countries. Students commonly place the reversible-borders sentence first because it sounds like a defining feature — address this by asking which came first in the passage's timeline. Three to four readings is the NCF guidance for listening tasks at this stage; do not shorten to fewer.

periods.activity_title: Synonyms and Odd-One-Out: Word Groups from the Chapter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p. 129): odd-one-out across four word sets; students also create two original synonym sets.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: smiling, grinning, laughing, crying. She asks: 'These are all words from stories about people — which one does not belong with the others and why?' Students respond, arriving at the idea of synonym groups with one intruder.

Let us Learn A (p. 129) — teacher writes all four sets on the board: (1) sad, unhappy, tearful, thrilled; (2) talk, discuss, kind, speak; (3) noisy, quiet, silent, calm; (4) cotton, wooden, silk, woollen. Students circle the odd one out in their textbooks and justify their answer orally for each set.

Students work in pairs to create two original synonym sets of their own, each with one odd-one-out intruder. Teacher circulates, asking pairs to read their sets aloud quietly and checking that the three synonym words genuinely share meaning.

Three or four pairs share their invented sets. The rest of the class identifies the odd one out and explains why. Teacher briefly revisits the chapter context: the words kindness, majestic, and fierce appear in Chachi's description — can students place them in a synonym group?

periods.teacher_notes: Set 3 (noisy, quiet, silent, calm) trips many students because quiet and calm can feel synonymous; guide them to see that noisy is the lone member of a different semantic cluster. The extension — creating their own sets — is the higher-order move; allow pairs enough time to think before writing. Students who finish early can challenge the class with a fifth set.

periods.activity_title: Silent 'g' and Word Meanings: Two Word-Work Tasks

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p. 130): identify silent 'g' words from a given list.
Let us Learn C (p. 130): match seven chapter vocabulary words to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn B (p. 130) — teacher writes design on the board and says it aloud, then writes DESIGN again with the g struck through. She explains that some letters appear in spelling but make no sound. Students read the nine words on p. 130 aloud together: sign, light, goat, night, sing, sugar, king, high, magnet.

Let us Learn B (p. 130) — students underline the silent-g words individually in their textbooks. Teacher then does a quick round-robin: each student says one word and the class claps if it has a silent g, stays silent if it does not. Correct answers: sign, light, night, high.

Let us Learn C (p. 130) — teacher reads the seven chapter words aloud: Kindness, Bravery, Wisdom, Majestic, Unique, Fierce, Dedicated. For each, she uses it in a sentence drawn from Chachi's description of Queen Ahilya Bai. Students then match columns A and B in their textbooks.

Pairs check each other's matching. Teacher projects or writes the answer key on the board. Students correct and then choose two of the seven words and use each in a new sentence about something or someone they know — share two or three with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently mark 'king' and 'sing' as silent-g words because they see the letter g — emphasise that in those words the g is part of the 'ng' sound and is pronounced, not silent. For the matching task, the words Majestic and Fierce often get swapped; ground each in a moment from the dialogue (Chachi calls the fort majestic; she calls the queen fierce in battle) to anchor meaning in context.

periods.activity_title: Articles in Context: A, An, and The in a Story Passage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak B (p. 132): fill in articles (a, an, the) throughout a short passage about a monkey.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes three sentences on the board with blanks: 'I saw ___ elephant. ___ elephant was eating ___ apple.' She asks students which article fits each blank and elicits the rule: a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds, the for something already known to both speaker and listener.

Let us Speak B (p. 132) — teacher reads the full monkey passage aloud with blanks clearly paused. Students follow in their textbooks. They then complete all blanks individually, working through the passage sentence by sentence.

Students compare answers with a partner and negotiate any differences. Teacher selects six blanks that commonly cause errors (once upon ___ time; ___ old man; ___ apple vs ___ pear) and works through each on the board, asking students to explain their choice.

Teacher reads the completed passage aloud with the correct articles inserted. Students follow and self-correct. She asks: 'Did the article change when the monkey mentioned the bag the second time? Why?' — connecting the exercise to the textbook context.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'once upon a time' is an idiom students may already know — use it as a confidence-builder at the start rather than a stumbling block. The most frequent error at this level is using 'a' before words beginning with a vowel sound (a apple, a olive) — address it by having students say the word aloud before choosing the article. A student who finishes early can write two new sentences using each article type.

periods.activity_title: Picture Yourself There: Descriptive Writing About Maheshwar Fort

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 133): write a short description imagining a visit to Maheshwar Fort with family.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits three vivid details from Chachi's description — the overhanging balconies of red stone, the Narmada River below the hill, and the 13-foot statue — by reading the relevant lines from pp. 125–128 aloud. She then asks students to close their eyes and imagine arriving at the fort.

Modelling: teacher thinks aloud as she writes one opening sentence and two descriptive sentences on the board, showing how to use sensory detail (what you see, hear, feel) and chapter vocabulary (majestic, unique, overhanging balconies). Students suggest words to add.

Let us Write A (p. 133) — students write their own descriptions independently. Teacher circulates, prompting quieter students with: 'What do you see first? What is one thing you feel as you walk inside?' She encourages use of the chapter's descriptive vocabulary.

Three or four students share their descriptions with the class. Classmates offer one positive observation each. Teacher underlines one strong phrase from each reading on the board as a collective vocabulary harvest.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task asks students to imagine visiting the fort — it is creative and personal, so there is no single correct content; assess for sensory detail, use of at least one chapter detail (balconies, river, statue, or temples), and sentence clarity. Students who write only one sentence need the oral scaffolding step again — ask them to say what they see before writing it. Peer-sharing at the close builds confidence and enriches vocabulary for those who wrote less.

periods.activity_title: Fact Paragraph and Fort Puzzle: Writing and Making

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 133): write a short factual paragraph about Maheshwar Fort using lesson details.
Let us Do (p. 134): make a fort jigsaw puzzle on cardboard, cut it, and reassemble with a partner.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write B (p. 133) — teacher writes a three-part paragraph frame on the board: (1) Where is Maheshwar Fort and who built it? (2) What are its special features? (3) Why is it important to people today? Students draft their factual paragraph in notebooks using the frame and their textbook notes.

Students exchange notebooks with a partner and check: Does the paragraph mention Queen Ahilya Bai? Does it name at least one building material or feature? Is there a sentence about the fort's importance? Partners mark any missing part. Students revise and complete their final version.

Let us Do (p. 134) — teacher distributes thick paper or chart offcuts. Students draw a simple fort outline on the back, draw a puzzle grid of six to eight pieces on the front, cut along the grid lines with safe scissors, mix the pieces, and reassemble. Teacher circulates and assists with cutting.

Students swap their puzzle pieces with a neighbour and try to assemble the neighbour's fort. Teacher asks: 'What made rearranging the pieces tricky? What helped you figure out where each piece belonged?' — connecting the hands-on experience to the idea of putting a story together piece by piece.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task is factual, not imaginative — students should draw on verified details from the dialogue (Madhya Pradesh, Queen Ahilya Bai, red stones from Gujarat and Rajasthan, the Narmada River, temples and wells) rather than personal feelings. Keep the paragraph frame visible on the board throughout the writing time so students have a structure to follow. For the puzzle craft, pre-cutting the paper into A5 sized rectangles saves time; if scissors are scarce, students may score the puzzle lines and tear carefully.
materials: Thick paper or chart offcuts (A5 per student)

periods.activity_title: Maheshwar Revisited: A Whole-Chapter Celebration and Oral Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p. 132): each student presents a short oral report on a historical place from their own locality.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking: 'What do you now know about Maheshwar that you did not know before this chapter?' Students call out facts freely — fort location, Queen Ahilya Bai, building stones, Maheshwari sarees, the statue. Teacher maps the responses into four clusters on the board: Place · Queen · Craft · Architecture.

Teacher displays — or asks a student to read aloud — one sentence that uses a word studied in the word-work strand: 'The queen was majestic, unique, and dedicated to her people.' She asks the class to swap any two of those words for near-synonyms from memory, reinforcing contextual vocabulary.

Let us Speak A (p. 132) — each student gives a brief oral presentation (one to two minutes) on a historical place in their town or nearby area, covering: name of the place, historical people connected to it, one special feature, and why it matters to local people. Teacher keeps a simple checklist on the board. Students listen and may ask one question after each presentation.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks connecting what they heard in the oral presentations to what Chachi described about Maheshwar — two things that are similar across historical places, and one thing that makes Maheshwar unique. This is a brief independent response, not a full essay.

Teacher closes the chapter by reading Chachi's final promise from p. 128: that they will all visit Maheshwar to discover its secrets. She asks the class: 'After everything you have read, discussed, listened to and made — what secret would you most want to discover?' One or two students respond orally, ending the chapter on a note of curiosity.

periods.teacher_notes: The oral presentation in this unit draws on information students have gathered about a local historical place — they need a few minutes at the start to organise their thoughts; the board clusters from the opening move give them a template. Students who have not been able to gather information beforehand can speak about Maheshwar Fort itself, using what the chapter taught them. The closing written response (three sentences) is intentionally brief — its purpose is to consolidate, not to produce a new piece of extended writing.

items.source_context: Aarav, Ananya, and Chachi discuss Maheshwar Fort, Queen Ahilya Bai, building materials, the Narmada River, and the fort's statue.
items.item_stem: Read the part of the dialogue where Chachi describes the fort's location. Which one of the following best describes where Maheshwar Fort stands?

options.label: A
options.text: Inside a valley below the Narmada River in Gujarat.

options.label: B
options.text: On a hill overlooking the Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh.

options.label: C
options.text: On a hilltop near the coast of Gujarat.

options.label: D
options.text: On the banks of the Yamuna River in Rajasthan.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have confused the source states of the building stones (Rajasthan/Gujarat) with the fort's actual location in Madhya Pradesh.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has blended two facts — Gujarat as a stone source and the fort's hilltop position — without fixing the correct state.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has the river right but reversed the fort's relationship to it; the fort looks down on the Narmada, it is not below it.

items.item_stem: In the dialogue, Chachi describes Queen Ahilya Bai and the statue that stands in front of the palace. In two or three sentences, explain who Queen Ahilya Bai was and what the statue of her represents, using details from the chapter.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Queen Ahilya Bai was a warrior queen of the Holkar family who ruled Maheshwar with kindness and wisdom. She built temples, schools, and wells for her people. The 13-feet tall statue standing in front of the palace represents the respect and remembrance the people hold for her.

items.item_stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short passage about Maheshwari sarees. Then choose the correct answer. According to the passage, what were Maheshwari sarees originally made of?

options.label: A
options.text: A blend of silk and cotton from the start.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have associated cotton with Maheshwari sarees without attending to the passage's distinction between the original and later materials.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the later blended form with the original; the passage says cotton was introduced after the sarees began as pure silk.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has introduced wool, which does not appear in the passage at all, suggesting attention was lost during listening.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Standing on the overhanging balconies, a visitor can look down at the wide Narmada River flowing far below and feel the cool breeze from the water.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may not recognise that brave, bold and fierce share the meaning of strength or courage, making brave part of the group, not the odd one out.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Bold belongs to the same cluster of strength words as brave and fierce; choosing it suggests the student focused on spelling rather than meaning.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fierce belongs to the courage-and-strength group along with brave and bold; choosing it suggests the student associated it only with aggression, missing the shared cluster.
